The trial enrolled 12 patients across melanoma, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), renal cell carcinoma (RCC), and microsatellite instability-high pancreatic cancer. The co-primary endpoints were safety and objective response rate (ORR). The study found that FMT was safe and feasible but demonstrated limited clinical activity: no objective responses were observed (ORR 0%), median progression-free survival was 1.5 months, and median overall survival was 10.1 months. Statistically significant associations (p<0.05) are annotated with an asterisk. n=11. PFS, progression-free survival; OS, overall survival. In this study, FMT from ICI responders was used to assess if gut microbiota modulation could overcome established ICI resistance in different cancer types. All patients had progressed on ICIs in the metastatic setting. We found that the study interventions had an acceptable safety profile, and that FMT was feasible in patients with advanced cancer, but observed no objective responses. A patient with melanoma had clinical benefit as defined in the protocol, with stable disease lasting more than 6 months, and remains alive after 33 months. Another patient with melanoma, who had no prior response or toxicity to ICIs, developed both evidence of response and immune-related toxicity, but eventually progressed and died. There has to our knowledge been no previous reports on FMT in HNSCC. In our trial, the patient with HNSCC had stable disease for 20 weeks and remains alive after 16 months. The potential risk of transmission of infectious agents is a concern with FMT.^{31} However, FMT has for decades been used for Clostridioides difficile infections, and the available data indicate that most FMT-related AEs are low-grade and self-limiting.^{32} Previous trials have indicated that FMT is safe also in patients with cancer,18,2033 and the results from our trial, MITRIC, support the safety of FMT in patients with advanced cancer. All AEs related to FMT treatment were grade 1, while one grade 3 event was recorded following colonoscopy. IrAEs occurred in 50% of patients and were mostly mild. Five out of six patients with irAEs in MITRIC had also experienced irAEs prior to study enrollment, suggesting that FMT did not increase the risk of irAEs. We furthermore found that irAEs were related to higher baseline PBMC levels of differentiated CD4+T cells with an EM and Th1 phenotype, as well as Tregs and ICOS^{+} CD8 T cells. This observation suggests that a pre-existing activated immune milieu may predispose to irAEs. However, from our dataset, it cannot be determined whether this phenotype was induced by prior ICI exposure. Previous single-arm studies have reported a potential for FMT to reverse ICI resistance. Two proof-of-concept trials in metastatic melanoma demonstrated clinical benefit in patients with anti-PD-1-refractory disease: Baruch et al^{19} reported objective responses in 3 of 10 patients, and Davar et al^{18} reported responses in 3 of 15 patients, with durable stable disease in three additional patients. Kim et al^{20} observed objective responses in 1 of 13 patients with upper gastrointestinal cancers progressing on PD-1 inhibition. FMT combined with ICIs is also being evaluated in the first-line setting. Recently, several single-arm studies have evaluated healthy-donor FMT in combination with anti-PD-1 monotherapy or anti-PD-1 plus anti-CTLA-4 therapy as first-line treatment in advanced melanoma,^{36 37} advanced non-small cell lung cancer^{36} and metastatic RCC.^{34} These studies suggest that FMT may enhance the efficacy of ICIs in the treatment-naïve setting. In addition, results from the randomized TACITO trial were recently published,^{35} indicating potential clinical activity of FMT combined with first-line anti-PD-1 therapy and a tyrosine kinase inhibitor in metastatic RCC, using ICI responders as donors. Various factors may explain the discrepancy between encouraging findings from previous FMT studies and the absence of confirmed responses in MITRIC. First, the small sample size represents an important limitation, as in earlier FMT trials conducted in ICI-resistant disease. Second, heterogeneity across studies—including differences in donor selection, FMT preparation, route of administration, and treatment schedule—may influence clinical and biological outcomes. Patient selection is also likely critical. In the studies by Baruch et al, Davar et al, and Kim et al, most responses occurred relatively late and were sometimes preceded by pseudo-progression, suggesting that patients with rapidly progressive disease and short expected survival may not be optimal candidates.18,20 In MITRIC, most patients presented with disseminated, fast-growing disease, which may not have allowed sufficient time for FMT to exert meaningful effects. We included both patients with and without previous ICI benefit, and it remains unclear in which clinical context microbiota modulation is most relevant. The recently accumulating first-line evidence,^{34 36 37} including randomized data,^{35} raises the possibility that the ICI-naïve setting may be better suited for FMT strategies. Donor characteristics are also likely crucial. As in other trials of ICI-refractory disease, we used long-term ICI responders as stool donors; however, microbial composition varies considerably among such donors, and it is unknown whether this approach is superior to using healthy donors. The small number of available donors adds uncertainty. Notably, all responders in Baruch et al received stool from a single donor,^{19} whereas our study used three donors, raising the possibility of suboptimal donor-recipient matching or lack of specific microbial communities required for benefit. Donor age may also influence microbial diversity, although older donors were likewise used in Davar et al.^{18} Finally, microbiota composition is shaped by diet, geography, medications, and host factors, contributing to inconsistent “beneficial” signatures across studies.^{13 14} Thus, FMT may be effective only in selected populations, and the gut microbiota represents just one of several determinants of immunotherapy outcome; reliable biomarkers to identify patients most likely to benefit from microbiota modulation have not yet been established. The MITRIC trial used repeated FMT treatments, under the premise that this should increase engraftment and thus the possibility of clinical success. The gut microbiota in most recipients shifted towards their respective donors 1 week after the first FMT, but this effect seemed transient in most recipients. As the patients progressed, it was not feasible to collect stool samples at later time points to assess long-term engraftment and the effects of repeated FMTs. One patient had long-term engraftment and, intriguingly, this was the only patient with clinical benefit in the study. This is in line with FMT studies in melanoma that have suggested long-term donor-recipient similarities only in responders.^{33} The PBMC data suggest that in this patient population, a highly differentiated T-cell environment is associated with improved PFS and OS, while a myeloid skewed and Th2-like environment suggests a poor prognosis. These findings are in line with existing knowledge on cancer immunity,^{4 38} and may reflect that these patients are treated with ICIs, which relies on the host immune response for their efficacy. The OS times calculated from the start of ICI therapy support that these observations represent immunological characteristics prognostic for patients treated with ICIs, and are not related to the FMT intervention. In particular, granzyme B^{+} CD8^{+} T cells were associated with favorable outcomes. Using the same mass cytometry panel, we recently identified this particular subset to be associated with clinical benefit from ICIs in a randomized breast cancer study.^{26} The FMT in MITRIC did not appear to induce changes in the systemic immune milieu, as measured by peripheral PBMC phenotypes. It would be of interest to explore if other FMT protocols or microbiota interventions could alter the PBMC signatures, and if this is related to clinical efficacy from FMT. Davar et al found that the clinical responders exhibited higher levels of CD56+CD8+ T cells in PBMCs after FMT/anti-PD-1 treatment, and that this subset expressed higher levels of various activation markers.^{18} Furthermore, Davar et al reported that responding patients had decreased circulating IL-8 and decreased frequencies of IL-8-producing myeloid cells in tumors. In contrast, we observed an increase in CD14^{+} monocytes and IL-8 during the study. Moreover, higher CD14^{+} monocyte levels after 4 weeks were in MITRIC associated with shorter PFS and OS. It is possible that increasing myeloid-driven immunosuppression in our patients during the course of the trial was related to the lack of benefit from FMT. However, the exploratory PBMC and cytokine data were not corrected for multiple testing in this study, and these findings should be interpreted with caution given the limited sample size. In conclusion, the MITRIC trial demonstrated that FMT in combination with ICIs is safe and feasible in patients with advanced cancers. While indications of clinical activity were observed in a few patients, FMT did not result in objective clinical responses in patients refractory to ICIs. Further research is needed to clarify whether FMT can enhance ICI efficacy, optimize FMT protocols, and establish criteria for donor and recipient selection. Microbiota sequencing received infrastructure support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG Excellence Cluster 2167 “Precision Medicine in Chronic Inflammation” and DFG Research Unit 5042 “miTarget”). Provenance and peer review: Not commissioned; externally peer reviewed. Patient consent for publication: Not applicable.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial in patients with metastatic renal cell carcinoma treated with anti-PD-1 plus a VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, donor fecal microbial transplantation (FMT) from complete responders to immunotherapy did not significantly improve the primary endpoint of 12-month progression-free survival (PFS) but did significantly improve median PFS versus placebo FMT. Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICIs) have changed the management of different cancers, including melanoma, non-small cell lung cancer and renal cell carcinoma (RCC). The combination of pembrolizumab (a programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) inhibitor monoclonal antibody) with axitinib (a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor (VEGFR) tyrosine kinase inhibitor) has significantly improved overall survival, progression-free survival (PFS) and objective response rate (ORR) in patients with metastatic RCC (mRCC)^{1}, and it is currently used as first-line therapy in this population. However, most patients experience disease progression within 16 months, with limited therapeutic options thereafter. A growing body of evidence suggests that the composition of the gut microbiome may affect the efficacy of ICIs in several epithelial tumors, including RCC^{2}. First, the use of antibiotics, which are known to disrupt the gut microbiome^{3}, has been associated with worse clinical response to ICIs in different types of cancer^{4}, including RCC^{5}. Also, several microbial taxa and/or ecological communities have been associated with response to ICIs in different epithelial cancers^{2}, and the transfer of gut microbiome from humans to mice was proven to influence the response to ICIs in cancer mouse models^{6}. Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) provided clinical benefit in ICI-refractory^{7–9} or treatment-naive^{10} patients with advanced solid tumors, mostly melanoma, without serious adverse events (SAEs). However, thus far, no randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have demonstrated the efficacy of FMT in mRCC. Our phase 2a placebo-controlled RCT aims to evaluate whether FMT from patients with mRCC with complete response to ICIs was effective in improving response to combined first-line therapy with pembrolizumab and axitinib in patients with mRCC. In this double-blind, placebo-controlled, investigator-initiated phase 2a RCT, we enrolled patients with metastatic, histologically confirmed RCC who were eligible to receive pembrolizumab and axitinib as first-line therapy. We excluded patients unable to undergo FMT, with a history of concomitant gastrointestinal or autoimmune disorders, with prior exposure to systemic immunomodulators or with ongoing or recent (<4 weeks prior to enrollment) antibiotic use. Full eligibility criteria are described in Methods. The primary endpoint was the rate of patients free from disease progression at 12 months after randomization (12-month PFS). Secondary endpoints were median PFS and median overall survival, ORR, safety and microbiome changes, after randomization. After a baseline visit, patients were randomized 1:1 to receive donor FMT (d-FMT) or placebo FMT (p-FMT) three times in 6 months, unless disease progression occurred. Both groups underwent the first procedure by colonoscopy, followed by capsulized FMT after 12 weeks and 24 weeks, respectively.

paper_context.opening: Fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) has shown promise in overcoming resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in early-phase cancer trials. We investigated the safety, feasibility and efficacy of FMT from ICI responders to patients with advanced cancers progressing on ICIs. This was a single-arm phase IIa basket trial (MITRIC; NCT05286294) including patients with ICI-refractory cancer. Long-term ICI responders were used as FMT donors. Patients received FMTs in combination with ICIs; two FMT administrations (by colonoscopy) were scheduled before the first radiological evaluation after 6 weeks, and up to three later FMTs were allowed (by enema). Co-primary endpoints were the evaluation of FMT-related adverse events and objective response rate. allowed (by enema). payload.user_scope: How does the gut microbiome modulate the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors in solid tumours, and what mechanisms mediate that effect?

system_prompt:
你是综述作者的材料阅读助手，围绕一个写作问题提炼具体研究认识。
一起阅读 material_found 和 paper_context，保留研究对象或材料、研究设置、比较对象、方法、操作或条件（如有）、结果或论证、验证方式与适用边界。卡片、专家综述转述和原文都按内容是否能回答问题使用，不因形式自动降权。
先理解 user_scope 与问题对象，不能用其他对象、方法、设置或比较冒充本问题的答案。特定模型、材料或场景的结果不得无依据外推到别的对象或设置；观察关联不改写为因果关系；统计或分析方法也不自动证明因果、排除混杂或完成独立验证，方法意义只说材料明确说明的部分。
输出 usable_content 为一段可直接阅读的字符串：适合本节的具体认识、研究异同、解释和条件。先呈现能区别不同研究的发现或论证，不先套领域常见结论；结尾也要保留这些区别。别把多个不同对象、材料、产品、场景或实验设置的结果合成一个普适机制或结论。
涉及数字时，先逐项输出 quantitative_comparisons，每项写 research_object、result_or_measure、setting_or_time、groups；groups 是 [{group:原文组名或缩写,value:紧邻该组的结果含单位}]，保留原文分组顺序与缩写，不重新命名或调序；缩写定义另写 group_definitions。逐字读取每个组名紧随的数值，不从常识、总体结论或组名列表反推配对。reported_statistics 记录原文给出的统计量（没报告才留空）。一组一数成对，不用多组名字对应一串数字；总体与分层比较、不同指标或结果分别记录。usable_content 解释含义，不重复重排数字。原文没有的值不编。问题限定某设置、时间或子组时，必须分别读总体和指定部分，不能拿总体结果代替，也不能把分析时点当成条件发生时点。
decision 判断当前具体问题是否解决，而不是材料有没有用：direct_use=足以回答当前问题，或有明确材料纠正其错误前提；local_deep_read=本地有材料但需要读另一部分或完整比较（read_focus 说明具体要读什么）；external_research=缺新的研究对象、方法、比较或验证材料（external_ask 提出保留对象和关系的窄需求）。external_research 也可以有丰富 usable_content：已有背景可用但核心问题没回答，就先保留内容并提出剩余检索需求。不要因为找到相关材料就宣布 direct_use。问题里的预设（例如研究阶段、设计、测量或效果）不是事实，先以材料校正。
对于“是否已经有某类研究/结果”的问题，找到一个符合条件的实例可以回答；几篇论文未提到，或一篇较早综述说当时没有，不能回答当前是否存在。已有内容可以说明截至该来源时间的研究格局；若仍需确认后来是否出现目标研究，就选择 external_research 并提出该项具体检索，不要一边宣布问题已解决一边仍要求确认其核心答案。只有问题明确限定在这些来源的时间或材料范围内，才可据此直接给出否定答案。
answers_requested_question 只表示当前材料是否真正回答了原问题和 success_criteria；有用但只覆盖背景或部分条件的内容填 false，明确的实验性阴性结果或明确限于这些来源/时间范围的否定答案可填 true。
reading_mode=focused_local_read 时已经执行补读，尽力完成具体认识；仍缺新材料则指出缺口，不循环要求读同一材料。摘要能回答背景或明确比较就可用，不强制全文。
先完成 quantitative_comparisons，再写 usable_content。必须先逐组读原句，不根据总体方向猜测分组方向；结果可以与提问隐含的方向相反。某部分出现反向或无差异时，综合开头就写清不同设置或对象结果不一致，不能先说“一致”再在后面补相反数据。同一指标的总体比较和按条件分层不是同一组数据，不得互换。
返回 JSON，按此顺序写字段：quantitative_comparisons（无数字则 []）, usable_content, decision, answers_requested_question（必须是 JSON boolean；不能确定或 success_criteria 未满足时填 false）, still_missing, read_focus, external_ask, reason。
